scenarios.title: Start Here: Ground Floor configuration review
scenarios.situation: Reviewing a Start Here: Ground Floor configuration before production. Something looks off.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most important misconfiguration to check?
choices: Security settings: overly permissive access is the most common and dangerous misconfiguration
Performance tuning: suboptimal but rarely critical at deploy
Naming conventions: annoying but not dangerous
Documentation: a problem but not a deployment blocker
scenarios.why: Security misconfigurations create immediate vulnerability. Verify auth, authz, encryption first. In LLM Engineering, working-but-insecure is worse than delayed-but-secure.
scenarios.hint: What causes the most damage if wrong?

scenarios.title: Start Here: Ground Floor performance issue
scenarios.situation: Users report Start Here: Ground Floor is slow. It was fast last week. No config changes made.
choices: Check resource utilization and data/traffic growth: regressions without config changes mean resource exhaustion or growth
Roll back to last week's backup
scenarios.why: Without config changes, causes are resource pressure or data growth. Check metrics first. Restarting masks problems; timeouts treat symptoms.
scenarios.hint: If config did not change, what did?

scenarios.title: Start Here: Ground Floor failure diagnosis
scenarios.situation: A critical Start Here: Ground Floor component failed. Diagnose quickly to restore service.
choices: Reproduce and scope, check logs/metrics, isolate the layer, hypothesize, test fix, verify
Try the most common fix first
scenarios.why: Systematic order preserves evidence and avoids wasted effort. Skipping to common fixes fails on uncommon issues; restarts destroy diagnostics.
scenarios.hint: Which approach preserves evidence?

scenarios.title: Start Here: Ground Floor design decision
scenarios.situation: Designing new Start Here: Ground Floor: simple (current needs) vs comprehensive (future scale).
choices: Start simple with clear extension points; avoid both under- and over-engineering
scenarios.why: Balance current needs with likely evolution. Ask: what is the cost of being wrong in each direction?
scenarios.hint: What balances the extremes?

scenarios.title: Start Here: Ground Floor security incident
scenarios.situation: Monitoring shows suspicious Start Here: Ground Floor activity. Might be attack or false positive.
choices: Contain first (isolate, preserve evidence), then investigate in parallel
scenarios.why: Contain to prevent spread while preserving forensics (isolate network, do not power off). Shutdowns destroy evidence; ignoring alerts breeds breaches.
scenarios.hint: How to balance stopping threat vs preserving evidence?

scenarios.title: Start Here: Ground Floor scaling challenge
scenarios.situation: Start Here: Ground Floor must handle 10x traffic next quarter.
choices: Measure bottlenecks, scale the constrained resource; verify, repeat
scenarios.why: Data-driven targeted scaling: load test, find bottlenecks, scale specifically, verify next constraint. Uniform scaling wastes resources; rewrites are risky.
scenarios.hint: Why targeted over uniform scaling?

choices: Attention — each token computes weighted relevance to every other token (Q·K scores, softmax, ×V), letting the model resolve 'it' from distant context; the cost is quadratic in sequence length
Attention just averages all tokens equally
scenarios.hint: To resolve 'it' in 'the trophy didn't fit the suitcase because it was too big' — which earlier tokens must the model consult?
scenarios.situation: A team treats the transformer as a black box. Asked why long documents cost more, they guess 'bigger model'.
scenarios.title: The attention intuition
scenarios.why: Attention lets every token weigh every other token: queries match keys (relevance scores), softmax normalizes to weights, values carry the content — a weighted sum of context. That's how 'it' binds to 'trophy'. Cost: every-token-to-every-token = O(n²) in sequence length — the reason long contexts are expensive and why efficient-attention variants exist. Attention is the context-resolution engine.

choices: Tokens — subword units (BPE); ~4 chars/token in English, more per token in code/CJK; context window = max tokens in+out; costs and latency scale with tokens
Context window is unlimited in practice
scenarios.hint: Why does the same paragraph cost 3x more in Japanese than English?
scenarios.prompt: What are tokens, and why do they govern cost?
scenarios.situation: A budget estimate assumes 'per request' pricing. Actual bills scale with input+output length, and CJK content costs more per character.
scenarios.title: The token bill
scenarios.why: Models process tokens (subword pieces), not characters: English ≈ 4 chars/token; code and CJK languages tokenize less efficiently (more tokens per character). Pricing, latency, and context limits are all per-token — input + output. Budgeting 'per request' is fiction; estimate tokens per request × volume. And the context window caps input+output combined — long inputs leave less room for answers.

choices: Temperature scales the logits before sampling: low → deterministic/greedy, high → diverse/creative; top-p (nucleus) truncates to the smallest set covering probability p — use low temp for factual tasks, higher for brainstorming
Top-p and temperature do the same thing
scenarios.hint: The support bot invents policies at temp 1.2 — which dial makes it stop improvising?
scenarios.situation: A support bot hallucinates at temperature 1.2. A brainstorming tool is boring at temperature 0.
scenarios.title: The sampling dials
scenarios.why: Temperature reshapes the probability distribution: →0 collapses to the most likely token (deterministic, factual); high flattens it (diverse, risky). Top-p samples from the smallest token set totaling probability p (cuts the long tail of weird tokens). Rule: factual/extraction/classification → temp 0–0.3; creative ideation → 0.7–1.0. They're the cheapest quality lever — tune before blaming the model.

choices: Embeddings — dense vectors where semantic similarity ≈ vector similarity (cosine); they power search, clustering, and RAG retrieval — but similarity isn't understanding
scenarios.hint: 'King − man + woman ≈ queen' — what does vector arithmetic capture?
scenarios.prompt: What are embeddings, and what do they enable?
scenarios.situation: A team wants semantic search over docs. They consider keyword matching 'good enough'.
scenarios.title: The meaning vectors
scenarios.why: Embeddings map text to dense vectors where distance ≈ meaning similarity — enabling semantic search ('refund policy' matches 'returns'), clustering, and RAG retrieval. Cosine similarity is the standard metric. Caveats: similarity is distributional (words appearing in similar contexts), not true understanding — 'hot' and 'cold' can embed nearby (both temperatures). Great for retrieval; not a reasoning engine.

choices: Pretraining learns language from raw text (next-token prediction); instruction tuning (SFT + RLHF/DPO) teaches following instructions and human preferences — the assistant behavior comes from the tuning, not the pretraining
scenarios.hint: A base model completes 'The capital of France is' — but does it answer 'What is the capital of France?' helpfully?
scenarios.prompt: What does each training stage contribute?
scenarios.situation: A team fine-tunes a base model (not instruct) for a chatbot and gets completions instead of answers.
scenarios.title: The two trainings
scenarios.why: Pretraining (next-token prediction on raw text) builds language/knowledge — the base model continues text. Instruction tuning (supervised fine-tuning on instruction-response pairs + preference optimization like RLHF/DPO) teaches the assistant behaviors: answering questions, refusing appropriately, formatting. Chatbots need instruct-tuned models; using a raw base model for dialogue is the classic mistake. Knowledge comes mostly from pretraining; behavior from tuning.

choices: Hallucination — fluent confabulation when the model lacks knowledge or the prompt underconstrains it; mitigate with grounding (RAG), constrained outputs, and verification — never trust ungrounded factual claims
Hallucinations mean the model is broken
Hallucination is just wrong training data
scenarios.hint: The model states a fake citation confidently — is that a bug, or the architecture working as designed?
scenarios.situation: An LLM cites papers that don't exist, with full confidence. The team calls it a bug to be patched.
scenarios.title: The confident liar
scenarios.why: Hallucination is architectural: next-token prediction optimizes for plausible continuation, not truth — the model has no truth register, only likelihood. Mitigations, not cures: ground with retrieved sources (RAG + citations), constrain outputs (schemas, allowed values), verify critical claims against sources, and set temperature low for factual tasks. Design systems assuming hallucination; verify anything that matters.

choices: Structure: role/task, context, explicit constraints, output format/schema, and examples — specificity beats cleverness; iterate against an eval set
evidence:
You are a support triage classifier.
Classify the ticket into exactly one of: [billing, technical, account].
Return JSON: {"category": "...", "confidence": 0.0-1.0}.
Ticket: ...
scenarios.hint: If the model returns prose instead of JSON, what was missing from the prompt?
scenarios.situation: A prototype prompt ('classify this ticket') returns inconsistent formats — prose, JSON, apologies.
scenarios.title: The flaky prompt
scenarios.why: Production prompts are specifications: role (who the model is), task (exactly what to do), constraints (the allowed categories — closed set), output schema (JSON shape — parseable), and edge handling. Vague prompts get vague outputs. Iterate like code: version prompts, test against cases, and constrain the output format so downstream parsing never breaks.

choices: Few-shot — show input→output examples in the prompt; worth the tokens when the format or judgment is hard to specify in words alone
Few-shot is obsolete with big models
scenarios.hint: 'Classify tone as: snarky, earnest, or bureaucratic' — easier to define in words, or to show?
scenarios.situation: A tone classifier's written definitions keep failing on edge cases. Three examples per class fix it.
scenarios.title: The examples that fixed it
scenarios.why: Few-shot shows the pattern: input→output pairs teach format, edge-case judgment, and style faster than prose definitions — especially for subjective tasks (tone, quality) where words underconstrain. Cost: tokens per request (examples ride along every call). Worth it when the task is hard to specify; skip when a clear rule + schema suffices. Choose diverse, representative examples — they define the decision boundary.

choices: Chain-of-thought — have the model reason step-by-step before answering (or use reasoning models); it improves multi-step accuracy but costs tokens and can rationalize wrong answers — verify the conclusion, not the story
scenarios.hint: 'Show your work' helps on math — but does the shown work prove the answer?
scenarios.prompt: When does step-by-step reasoning help, and what is its limit?
scenarios.situation: A model fails multi-step word problems with direct answers but solves them when asked to show work.
scenarios.title: The show-your-work prompt
scenarios.why: Chain-of-thought decomposes problems: intermediate steps reduce the per-step leap, improving arithmetic/logic accuracy. Techniques: 'think step by step', few-shot with worked examples, or reasoning models that do it natively. Limits: tokens and latency cost; and traces can be post-hoc rationalizations — a plausible story around a wrong answer. Verify conclusions independently for high stakes; CoT is a tool, not a proof.

choices: Golden eval set — fixed input/expected-output pairs + automated checks (exact match, schema validity, LLM-judge for open-ended) run on every prompt/model change; track regressions like tests
Eyeball a few outputs after each change
scenarios.hint: You changed one sentence in the prompt — how do you know nothing else broke?
scenarios.prompt: How do you know a prompt change helped?
scenarios.situation: A prompt tweak fixes one case and breaks three others. Nobody noticed for a week.
scenarios.title: The prompt regression
scenarios.why: LLM features need test suites: a golden set of representative inputs with expected behaviors, run automatically on every prompt/model/config change. Checks: deterministic (exact match, JSON schema valid, constraints held) where possible; LLM-as-judge with rubrics for open-ended quality (with judge-bias caveats). Without evals, prompt engineering is vibes. With them, it's engineering — regressions get caught like code regressions.

choices: Decompose: one focused prompt per subtask, chained (extract → validate → summarize), each with its own schema and eval — debuggable, testable, and each step uses the right model/size
One giant prompt — the model handles complexity
Chaining adds failure points; avoid it
Each step must use the same model
scenarios.hint: When the mega-prompt fails, which of its five jobs broke?
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle complex multi-step tasks?
scenarios.situation: A mega-prompt (extract entities, resolve them, summarize, format, translate) fails opaquely. No step is testable alone.
scenarios.title: The mega-prompt
scenarios.why: Decompose into a pipeline of focused prompts: each does one job with a strict I/O schema, each is independently evaluable, and each can use the right-sized model (small for extraction, large for judgment). Failures localize to a step; retries target the step. The mega-prompt optimizes for demo simplicity; chains optimize for debuggability and reliability. (Agents generalize this with dynamic chaining.)

choices: System prompt as the durable instruction layer (role, rules, constraints) + user prompt as the per-request input; keep secrets and policy in the system prompt, data in the user message — and remember neither is a security boundary
System prompts are hidden from users — safe for secrets
scenarios.hint: If the user writes 'ignore previous instructions', which layer should hold the rules that must survive?
scenarios.prompt: How do you split system vs user prompts?
scenarios.situation: API keys in the prompt leak via clever user inputs; instructions get overridden by pasted content.
scenarios.title: The prompt layers
scenarios.why: System prompt: durable directives (role, policy, output rules) — set by the developer, applied every turn. User prompt: the per-request data/task. Separation organizes behavior, but it's not a security boundary: prompt injection ('ignore instructions...') can override system directives via user content. So: never put real secrets in prompts (they can leak), validate tool calls server-side, and treat model-following-user-instructions as expected behavior to be constrained by architecture, not by prompt wishes.

choices: Chunking — split docs into retrievable units (e.g., 300-800 tokens with overlap, respecting structure like sections); too large dilutes relevance, too small loses context
scenarios.hint: A 50-page manual as one chunk — when the query matches one paragraph, what gets retrieved?
scenarios.prompt: Why is chunking the first RAG decision?
scenarios.situation: A RAG system over PDFs retrieves whole 50-page documents; answers are vague and context windows overflow.
scenarios.title: The 50-page chunk
scenarios.why: Retrieval returns chunks — the chunk is the unit of relevance. Whole documents dilute the match (one relevant paragraph in 50 pages scores weakly) and flood the context. Too-small chunks lose surrounding context ('it' refers to what?). Practice: structure-aware splits (sections, paragraphs), 300-800 tokens with overlap, metadata (source, page, date) attached for citations and filtering. Chunking quality bounds everything downstream.

choices: Retrieval metrics first: recall@k (did we fetch the right chunks?), then answer faithfulness (is every claim supported by cited chunks?) — evaluate retrieval and generation separately
End-to-end vibes — read a few answers
scenarios.hint: The answer is wrong — is the retriever fetching garbage, or is the generator ignoring good chunks?
scenarios.prompt: How do you evaluate a RAG system?
scenarios.situation: A RAG bot gives wrong answers. The team blames the LLM; the retriever fetches irrelevant chunks.
scenarios.title: The wrong layer
scenarios.why: Evaluate the two stages separately: retrieval (recall@k / precision@k against labeled relevant chunks — 'did we fetch the evidence?') and generation (faithfulness: every claim traceable to cited chunks; answer relevance). Fix the failing stage: bad retrieval → chunking/embeddings/hybrid search; bad generation → grounding prompts, citation requirements. End-to-end-only evals misattribute failures — instrument both.

choices: Grounding discipline: instruct the model to answer only from provided context, cite sources, and say 'not in the sources' when absent — plus verify citations resolve to real chunks
Tell the model to be confident
The model will naturally stay grounded
scenarios.hint: 'According to [3]...' — what if chunk [3] doesn't say that?
scenarios.prompt: How do you keep answers tied to sources?
scenarios.situation: A RAG bot answers from parametric memory instead of retrieved docs, citing sources that don't support the claims.
scenarios.title: The ungrounded answer
scenarios.why: RAG's promise is 'answer from these documents' — enforce it: prompt the model to use only provided context, require citations per claim, and define the abstention behavior ('I don't find this in the sources'). Then verify: citation faithfulness checks (does the cited chunk actually support the claim?) catch the confident-but-unfounded answers. Ungrounded RAG is just a chatbot with extra steps.

choices: Hybrid search — dense vectors (semantic) + BM25 keyword (exact terms, codes, names) fused (e.g., reciprocal rank fusion); dense alone misses exact identifiers
Dense vectors handle exact codes fine
Hybrid doubles cost with no benefit
scenarios.hint: Query: 'error XG-5021' — will semantic similarity find the exact code?
scenarios.prompt: When does pure vector search fail?
scenarios.situation: 'Where is error XG-5021 documented?' — vector search returns semantically similar errors, not the exact code.
scenarios.title: The exact-code query
scenarios.why: Dense embeddings capture meaning but blur exact tokens (part numbers, error codes, names). BM25/keyword search excels at exact matches. Hybrid fuses both (reciprocal rank fusion is standard) — semantic for concepts, keyword for identifiers. Technical/procedural corpora (full of codes and SKUs) need hybrid; pure prose Q&A can survive on dense alone. Know your corpus's query types.

choices: Metadata filtering + hierarchical retrieval — filter by source/date/type before vector search; retrieve coarse then fine (summary → chunks) for long docs
scenarios.hint: '2024 refund policy' — how do you avoid retrieving the 2021 policy?
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle time-sensitive or multi-source corpora?
scenarios.situation: A policy bot mixes 2021 and 2024 policies; answers cite outdated rules.
scenarios.title: The stale policy
scenarios.why: Attach metadata (source, date, doc type, version) at chunking time; filter pre-retrieval ('policy docs, effective 2024') so stale chunks never compete. Hierarchical retrieval (retrieve section summaries, then drill into chunks) handles long documents efficiently. Flat search over a mixed corpus is how 'the old policy' becomes the answer — structure the corpus, don't just embed it.

choices: Query rewriting / HyDE — transform the user query (expand, decompose, or generate a hypothetical answer to embed) because user phrasing rarely matches document phrasing
Embed the raw query always — simplest
scenarios.hint: User asks 'how do I get my money back'; the doc says 'refund disbursement procedure' — do those embed nearby?
scenarios.prompt: How do you bridge the phrasing gap?
scenarios.situation: Users phrase questions casually; docs use formal terminology. Retrieval misses.
scenarios.title: The vocabulary mismatch
scenarios.why: The query-document vocabulary gap kills retrieval: embed the raw casual query and it lands far from formal docs. Fixes: query rewriting (LLM expands/paraphrases the query), HyDE (generate a hypothetical answer, embed that — answers embed near answers), or multi-query (several phrasings, fuse results). The retrieval query is an engineering artifact — optimize it, don't just pass through the user's words.

choices: Decision tree: prompt engineering (format/behavior) → RAG (knowledge) → fine-tuning (style, domain patterns, consistent behavior at scale) — fine-tune when the behavior must be baked in across many calls, not for facts that change
scenarios.hint: The product catalog changes daily — should that knowledge live in weights or in retrieval?
scenarios.prompt: When is fine-tuning the right choice?
scenarios.situation: A team fine-tunes on the product catalog to answer product questions. The catalog updates daily; the model is stale within a week.
scenarios.title: The stale fine-tune
scenarios.why: Fine-tuning bakes patterns into weights: tone/style, domain jargon, task formats, consistent behavior — things stable over time. It's the wrong tool for changing facts (catalog, policies) — that's RAG's job (update the docs, not the weights). And for one-off behaviors, prompting is cheaper. Rule: stable behavior → fine-tune; changing knowledge → RAG; quick iteration → prompt. Fine-tuning for facts is the classic misapplication.

choices: LoRA — train low-rank adapter matrices injected into layers instead of all weights; QLoRA quantizes the base model to 4-bit so fine-tuning fits on one GPU — 1% of parameters, near-full quality
scenarios.hint: If the weight update is low-rank, how many parameters must you actually train?
scenarios.situation: Full fine-tuning needs 8 GPUs. The team has one.
scenarios.title: The one-GPU fine-tune
scenarios.why: LoRA freezes the base model and trains small low-rank matrices (rank r ≪ dimension) added to attention layers — ~0.1-1% of parameters, swappable adapters per task. QLoRA goes further: 4-bit quantized base + LoRA adapters → 65B-class models tunable on a single GPU. Near full-fine-tune quality for most tasks at a fraction of the cost. Full fine-tuning remains for deep capability changes; LoRA covers the rest.

choices: Instruction dataset quality > quantity — diverse, correct, representative examples of the desired behavior; garbage examples teach garbage behavior; evaluate on held-out tasks
More data always better regardless of quality
Dataset size is the only metric
Evaluation can be skipped for fine-tunes
scenarios.hint: 1,000 perfect examples vs 100,000 scraped noisy ones — which teaches the behavior?
scenarios.prompt: What matters in the fine-tuning dataset?
scenarios.situation: A fine-tune on 100k scraped Q&A pairs produces a worse assistant than the base instruct model.
scenarios.title: The noisy dataset
scenarios.why: Fine-tuning teaches behavior by example — noisy, incorrect, or off-style examples teach exactly that. Curate: correct answers, diverse phrasings, coverage of the target behaviors, and held-out eval tasks. A few thousand excellent examples beat a hundred thousand scraped ones (the LIMA finding: quality and diversity dominate). And eval before/after on the target tasks — fine-tuning can regress general abilities.

choices: Catastrophic forgetting — new training overwrites old capabilities; mitigate with mixed replay data (keep general examples in the mix), lower LR, and fewer epochs
scenarios.hint: After tuning on legal contracts, the model can't do basic math — what happened to the old weights?
scenarios.prompt: What is catastrophic forgetting, and how do you prevent it?
scenarios.situation: A customer-support fine-tune destroys the model's coding ability.
scenarios.title: The forgotten skills
scenarios.why: Gradient updates don't discriminate — training hard on one domain shifts weights away from others (forgetting). Defenses: mix general/replay data into training (don't train on the specialty alone), modest learning rates and epochs, and eval the preserved capabilities (regression suite on general tasks), not just the new skill. LoRA reduces but doesn't eliminate it. Fine-tuning is specialization — budget for what you might lose.

choices: Distillation — train a small model on a large model's outputs for the specific task; cheaper to serve, nearly as good on narrow tasks — the deploy-small strategy
Distillation copies the large model's weights
Small models can't learn from large ones
scenarios.hint: The 70B model is great but costs $X per 1M tokens — what if a 8B model learned just this task from it?
scenarios.prompt: How do you get big-model quality at small-model cost?
scenarios.situation: A 70B model nails classification; serving cost is prohibitive at scale.
scenarios.title: The expensive classifier
scenarios.why: Distillation: use the large model as a teacher — generate labeled outputs (often with rationales) on your task data, train the small student on them. The student learns the task-specific behavior at 1/10th the serving cost. Works best on narrow, well-defined tasks (classification, extraction, formatting). It's the standard 'prototype on big, deploy on small' pipeline — but check the teacher's license terms for distillation.

choices: Preference tuning (DPO/RLHF) — train on chosen vs rejected response pairs to align style/safety/helpfulness; it shapes preferences, not knowledge
scenarios.hint: SFT taught the format; how do you teach 'prefer the helpful, harmless answer'?
scenarios.prompt: What does preference tuning add on top of SFT?
scenarios.situation: An SFT model follows formats but gives blunt, sometimes unsafe answers. The team wants better judgment.
scenarios.title: The blunt assistant
scenarios.why: SFT (supervised fine-tuning) teaches 'how to respond' by example. Preference tuning (RLHF with a reward model, or DPO directly on chosen/rejected pairs) teaches 'which response is better' — aligning helpfulness, tone, and safety. DPO is the simpler modern path (no separate reward model/RL loop). It shapes preferences and style, not factual knowledge — don't expect it to teach the model new facts.

choices: ReAct — interleave reasoning traces with actions (tool calls) and observations; the model thinks, acts, sees the result, and continues — the foundation of tool-using agents
evidence:
Thought: I need the order status.
Action: get_order(order_id=42)
Observation: {status: 'shipped', ...}
Thought: Now I can answer...
scenarios.hint: Think → do → see → think again. What loop does that describe?
scenarios.situation: An agent must check an order, then a shipment, then answer — multi-step with dependencies.
scenarios.title: The think-act loop
scenarios.why: ReAct structures agents as Thought → Action → Observation loops: the model reasons about what it needs, calls a tool, incorporates the result, and repeats. The trace makes behavior debuggable (you see the plan evolve); the observations ground each step in reality instead of hallucinated tool results. It's the base pattern that planning, reflection, and multi-agent systems build on.

choices: Function/tool calling — the model emits structured calls (name + JSON args) the harness executes; validate args server-side, define narrow tools with clear schemas
Let the model emit raw SQL to execute
scenarios.hint: Who actually runs the tool — the model, or your code?
scenarios.prompt: How do models use tools safely?
scenarios.situation: An agent needs live data. The first version has the model write SQL directly.
scenarios.title: The tool interface
scenarios.why: Function calling: the model outputs a structured call; your harness validates and executes it. Design narrow tools with JSON schemas (get_order, not run_sql) — least privilege for agents. Validate arguments server-side (the model can be tricked into malicious args via prompt injection). The model proposes; your code disposes. Raw SQL/ shell from model output is an injection vulnerability wearing an agent costume.

choices: Bounded autonomy: explicit allowlists, action budgets (max steps/tool calls), human approval for irreversible actions, and kill switches — autonomy is a dial, not a switch
Full autonomy — the model is smart enough
Human review of every step is the only safety
scenarios.hint: The agent can refund, email, and delete — which of those should need a human?
scenarios.prompt: How do you bound an agent's actions?
scenarios.situation: A support agent issues refunds autonomously. One bug refunds $50k before anyone notices.
scenarios.title: The $50k refund
scenarios.why: Bound autonomy by blast radius: read-only tools run free; reversible writes (drafts) run with limits; irreversible actions (refunds, deletes, sends) require human approval or tight policy caps. Add action budgets (max N steps), timeouts, and audit logs of every action. The $50k bug is the tuition for 'the agent can do anything the API allows'. Autonomy without guardrails is just unreviewed code execution.

choices: Plan-then-execute for complex multi-step tasks (explicit plan, reviewed, then executed) vs reactive ReAct for dynamic environments — and replanning when observations invalidate the plan
scenarios.hint: Book a trip (plan first) vs debug a server (react to each finding) — which strategy each?
scenarios.prompt: When do agents plan ahead vs react step-by-step?
scenarios.situation: A research agent wanders without direction; a booking agent replans after every trivial observation.
scenarios.title: The planning question
scenarios.why: Plan-then-execute: generate the full plan, (optionally) get approval, execute steps — efficient for well-understood multi-step tasks. Reactive (ReAct): decide each step from observations — better for uncertain environments (debugging, research). Hybrid: plan, execute, replan when reality diverges. Match the strategy to uncertainty: known path → plan; unknown terrain → react. And surface the plan to the user for complex tasks — inspectability builds trust.

choices: Specialized subagents (researcher, coder, reviewer) coordinated by an orchestrator — parallelize independent work, separate concerns; but coordination overhead and context passing cost — use when tasks genuinely decompose
scenarios.hint: Research, code, and review — separable jobs, or one mind?
scenarios.prompt: When do multiple agents beat one?
scenarios.situation: A single agent juggles research, coding, and review — context overflows and quality drops per role.
scenarios.title: The overloaded agent
scenarios.why: Multi-agent: decompose into roles (researcher gathers, coder implements, reviewer critiques), orchestrated with clear handoffs. Wins: parallel work, focused contexts per role, separation of concerns (the reviewer isn't anchored by the coder's reasoning). Costs: coordination complexity, context-passing overhead, failure modes multiply. Use when the task genuinely decomposes and single-agent context/quality breaks down — not as default architecture.

choices: Reflection/self-critique loops — the agent reviews its own output against criteria and revises; bounded iterations, with the critic prompt separate from the generator
The same prompt can critique itself well
scenarios.hint: Draft, then 'review this draft against these 3 criteria, then revise' — what loop is that?
scenarios.prompt: How do agents improve their own outputs?
scenarios.situation: An agent's first-draft reports are mediocre. Human review of every draft doesn't scale.
scenarios.title: The self-review loop
scenarios.why: Reflection: generate → critique against explicit criteria (separate critic prompt, ideally a different model/temperature) → revise → repeat, bounded (2-3 rounds). It catches a real fraction of errors (format violations, missing requirements, inconsistencies). Limits: the critic shares the generator's blind spots; unbounded loops burn tokens and can degrade output. Use for quality-critical artifacts with clear rubrics — not as a substitute for ground-truth evals.

choices: VRAM math: ~2 bytes/param at 16-bit (70B ≈ 140 GB), ~0.5 bytes at 4-bit quant (70B ≈ 35 GB) + context overhead (KV cache grows with sequence length) — fit the quantized model to your GPU, or split across GPUs
scenarios.hint: 70B parameters × 2 bytes = ? And what does the KV cache add for 32k context?
scenarios.prompt: How do you know what fits on your hardware?
scenarios.situation: A team wants to run a 70B model on a single 24 GB GPU.
scenarios.title: The VRAM math
scenarios.why: Weights: params × bytes/param (FP16: 2, 8-bit: 1, 4-bit: 0.5) — 70B at 4-bit ≈ 35 GB > 24 GB, so it doesn't fit even quantized; a 32B at 4-bit (≈16 GB) fits with room for KV cache. Plus: KV cache scales with context length × layers — long context eats gigabytes. Do the arithmetic before downloading: (params × bytes) + KV cache + overhead < VRAM. No math, no model.

choices: Quantization levels: Q8 (near-lossless), Q6/Q5 (good balance), Q4 (standard for chat, small quality cost), Q3 and below (degrading) — pick the highest compression your quality evals tolerate
scenarios.hint: Q4 vs Q8 on your eval set — what decides?
scenarios.prompt: How do you choose a quantization level?
scenarios.situation: A Q4 model answers well but fails at precise JSON extraction; Q8 works but is slower.
scenarios.title: The quant tradeoff
scenarios.why: Quantization compresses weights (fewer bits/param): Q8 ≈ full quality, Q4_K_M the sweet spot for chat (minor degradation), Q3 and below visibly degrade (especially math, code, precise formats). The choice is empirical: run your eval set at each level, pick the smallest that passes. Task sensitivity varies — creative chat tolerates Q4; structured extraction may need Q5/Q6. Eval, don't guess.

choices: Inference servers: llama.cpp (CPU/GPU, single-node, simple), vLLM (high-throughput GPU serving, paged attention, continuous batching), Ollama (easy local dev) — match to scale: dev → Ollama, production GPU → vLLM
scenarios.hint: 1 user experimenting vs 100 concurrent API users — same server?
scenarios.prompt: How do you serve an open-weight model?
scenarios.situation: A prototype on Ollama needs to become a 50-req/s production API.
scenarios.title: The serving stack
scenarios.why: llama.cpp: efficient single-node inference (great for local/dev, GGUF quants, CPU offload). vLLM: production GPU serving — PagedAttention (memory-efficient KV cache) + continuous batching = high throughput for concurrent requests. Ollama: friendly local dev wrapper. The prototype-to-production path usually means moving from Ollama/llama.cpp to vLLM (or a managed endpoint) with load testing. Throughput is a server-architecture outcome, not just a model property.

choices: Licenses vary: Apache/MIT (do anything), Llama Community (broad use, with conditions), some with restrictions (non-commercial, copyleft-ish) — read the actual license for commercial use, especially redistribution and 'train on outputs' clauses
Licenses don't matter for internal use
scenarios.hint: 'Open weights' ≠ 'open source' — what did you actually agree to by downloading?
scenarios.prompt: What do you check before commercial use?
scenarios.situation: A startup builds on a model 'everyone uses'. Legal asks about the license; nobody read it.
scenarios.title: The license check
scenarios.why: Open weights ≠ OSI open source: licenses range from permissive (Apache 2.0/MIT) to custom community licenses with use conditions (attribution, acceptable-use policies, sometimes scale thresholds or redistribution terms). For commercial products: read the license, check redistribution/hosting terms, and verify whether training on the model's outputs is permitted. 'Everyone uses it' is not legal advice.

choices: Control/privacy/data-sovereignty vs cost/ops-burden: self-host when data can't leave, customization is deep, or scale makes API bills exceed ops cost — otherwise APIs win on simplicity
scenarios.hint: 1M requests/day of sensitive data — when does the GPU cluster beat the API bill?
scenarios.prompt: How do you decide self-host vs API?
scenarios.situation: A healthcare startup processes sensitive documents at high volume. API bills soar; compliance restricts data flow.
scenarios.title: The build-vs-buy
scenarios.why: Self-host wins on: data control (nothing leaves your VPC — compliance/privacy), predictable cost at scale (GPUs amortize vs per-token bills), and deep customization (fine-tunes, custom serving). APIs win on: zero ops, instant scaling, always-latest models. Model it: (tokens/day × API price) vs (GPU cost + engineering time). High-volume + sensitive + stable workload → self-host; variable/spiky + standard tasks → API. It's arithmetic plus risk tolerance.

choices: Eval on your task at each candidate (quality, latency, throughput, cost) — the 'best' model is task-relative; rerun evals when swapping models because behavior differs
scenarios.hint: Model A tops the leaderboard; model B is 5x cheaper and passes your evals — which ships?
scenarios.prompt: How do you choose which open model to run?
scenarios.situation: Three candidate models; the team argues from leaderboard scores.
scenarios.title: The leaderboard trap
scenarios.why: Leaderboards measure general benchmarks, not your task. Select empirically: define your task evals (quality bar, latency SLA, throughput need), run each candidate, and pick the smallest/cheapest that passes — then lock it with regression evals. Model behavior differs (instruction-following style, refusal patterns, format compliance), so every swap re-runs the evals. The right model is the cheapest one that clears your bar, not the highest-ranked one.

lessons.title: Transformer Basics — Core concepts
concepts: Attention lets every token weigh every other token: queries match keys (relevance scores), softmax normalizes to weights, values carry the content — a weighted sum of context.
Context resolution: pricing, latency, and context limits are all per-token — input + output.
Context windows: and the context window caps input+output combined — long inputs leave less room for answers.
Temperature reshapes the probability distribution: →0 collapses to the most likely token (deterministic, factual); high flattens it (diverse, risky).
Top-p samples from the smallest token set totaling probability p (cuts the long tail of weird tokens).

lessons.title: RAG — Core concepts
concepts: Chunking strategies: attach metadata (source, date, doc type, version) at chunking time; filter pre-retrieval ('policy docs, effective 2024') so stale chunks never compete. Chunking quality bounds everything downstream.

Retrieval metrics: fix the failing stage: bad retrieval → chunking/embeddings/hybrid search; bad generation → grounding prompts, citation requirements. Hierarchical retrieval (retrieve section summaries, then drill into chunks) handles long documents efficiently.

Hybrid search: technical/procedural corpora (full of codes and SKUs) need hybrid; pure prose Q&A can survive on dense alone. Flat search over a mixed corpus is how 'the old policy' becomes the answer — structure the corpus, don't just embed it.

lessons.title: Agent Architectures — Core concepts

Tool use: reAct structures agents as Thought → Action → Observation loops: the model reasons about what it needs, calls a tool, incorporates the result, and repeats. Use when the task genuinely decomposes and single-agent context/quality breaks down — not as default architecture.

lessons.title: LLM Engineering — Core concepts
concepts: Prompting is interface design: separate system instructions from user data, show the format with few-shot examples, and demand structured output with a schema instead of parsing prose.
Embeddings turn text into searchable geometry: chunk documents, embed them, and retrieve by cosine similarity — then generate from the retrieved context and cite it.
Fine-tuning changes behavior, not knowledge: use it (or parameter-efficient methods like LoRA) for consistent tone and format on stable tasks — reach for RAG when facts change often.
Agents are loops with tools: plan, act, observe — bounded by max steps, timeouts, and least-privilege tool access. An unbounded agent is an incident waiting to happen.
Measure everything: eval harnesses with temperature 0, golden sets, and regression runs on every prompt or model change — the model's mood is not a metric.

simulations.brief: The RAG system answers confidently but cites documents that do not contain the answer. Users are losing trust.
simulations.debrief: Faithfulness failures come from the generator ignoring the retrieved context — or retrieval returning junk the generator then dresses up. Fix retrieval relevance first, then constrain generation to cite only retrieved passages.

steps.explain: The generator is not the first suspect — retrieval is returning irrelevant chunks, and the model fills the gap with confident prose. Improve chunking and the reranker before touching the prompt.

sections.heading: Transformer Basics
items: Attention lets every token weigh every other token — queries match keys (relevance scores), softmax normalizes to weights, values carry the content — a weighted sum of context.
Context resolution — pricing, latency, and context limits are all per-token — input + output.
Context windows — and the context window caps input+output combined — long inputs leave less room for answers.
Temperature reshapes the probability distribution — →0 collapses to the most likely token (deterministic, factual); high flattens it (diverse, risky).
Top-p — Top-p samples from the smallest token set totaling probability p (cuts the long tail of weird tokens).
Common trap — cosine similarity measures exact matches.
Common trap — attention just averages all tokens equally.
Common trap — context window is unlimited in practice.
Common trap — tokenization doesn't affect cost.

Read — Read the setup and name the principle at play before looking at the reasoning. Then compare your answer with the takeaway — if they differ, re-read the concepts above and try the drill scenarios for this domain.

sections.heading: Prompting & Evals
items: Prompt design — system prompt: durable directives (role, policy, output rules) — set by the developer, applied every turn. Without evals, prompt engineering is vibes.

Output constraints — production prompts are specifications: role (who the model is), task (exactly what to do), constraints (the allowed categories — closed set), output schema (JSON shape — parseable), and edge handling.
Few-shot prompting — techniques: 'think step by step', few-shot with worked examples, or reasoning models that do it natively.
Chain-of-thought decomposes problems — intermediate steps reduce the per-step leap, improving arithmetic/logic accuracy.
Common trap — system prompts are hidden from users.
Common trap — chaining adds failure points; avoid it.
Common trap — prompt tricks and magic words.
Common trap — few-shot is obsolete with big models.

Production prompts are specifications — role (who the model is), task (exactly what to do), constraints (the allowed categories — closed set), output schema (JSON shape — parseable), and edge handling. Vague prompts get vague outputs. Iterate like code: version prompts, test against cases, and co…

sections.heading: RAG
items: Chunking strategies — attach metadata (source, date, doc type, version) at chunking time; filter pre-retrieval ('policy docs, effective 2024') so stale chunks never compete. Chunking quality bounds everything downstream.

RAG's promise is 'answer from these documents' — enforce it — prompt the model to use only provided context, require citations per claim, and define the abstention behavior ('I don't find this in the sources').

Retrieval metrics — fix the failing stage: bad retrieval → chunking/embeddings/hybrid search; bad generation → grounding prompts, citation requirements. Hierarchical retrieval (retrieve section summaries, then drill into chunks) handles long documents efficiently.
Citations — practice: structure-aware splits (sections, paragraphs), 300-800 tokens with overlap, metadata (source, page, date) attached for citations and filtering.

Hybrid search — technical/procedural corpora (full of codes and SKUs) need hybrid; pure prose Q&A can survive on dense alone. Flat search over a mixed corpus is how 'the old policy' becomes the answer — structure the corpus, don't just embed it.
Common trap — chunking doesn't affect retrieval.
Common trap — dense vectors handle exact codes fine.
Common trap — hybrid doubles cost with no benefit.
Common trap — the model will naturally stay grounded.

sections.heading: Fine-Tuning
items: Fine-tuning vs RAG — full fine-tuning remains for deep capability changes; LoRA covers the rest. Fine-tuning bakes patterns into weights: tone/style, domain jargon, task formats, consistent behavior — things stable over time.
LoRA — qLoRA goes further: 4-bit quantized base + LoRA adapters → 65B-class models tunable on a single GPU. LoRA reduces but doesn't eliminate it.
Parameter-efficient tuning — preference tuning (RLHF with a reward model, or DPO directly on chosen/rejected pairs) teaches 'which response is better' — aligning helpfulness, tone, and safety.
Common trap — more data always better regardless of quality.
Common trap — forgetting doesn't happen with LoRA.
Common trap — preference tuning teaches facts.
Common trap — distillation copies the large model's weights.

sections.heading: Agent Architectures
items: ReAct pattern — it's the base pattern that planning, reflection, and multi-agent systems build on. Reactive (ReAct): decide each step from observations — better for uncertain environments (debugging, research).

Tool use — reAct structures agents as Thought → Action → Observation loops: the model reasons about what it needs, calls a tool, incorporates the result, and repeats. Use when the task genuinely decomposes and single-agent context/quality breaks down — not as default…
Function calling — the model outputs a structured call; your harness validates and executes it.

Tool design — the trace makes behavior debuggable (you see the plan evolve); the observations ground each step in reality instead of hallucinated tool results. Design narrow tools with JSON schemas (get_order, not run_sql) — least privilege for agents.
Guardrails — autonomy without guardrails is just unreviewed code execution.
Common trap — reAct means reacting without thinking.
Common trap — let the model emit raw SQL to execute.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
For Transformer Basics: restate the 'why' behind each scenario answer in your own words — if you can't explain it, you don't own it.
Redo one Prompting & Evals lab from scratch without looking at the steps.
